title: The Sequential Criterion for Continuity
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A function f is continuous at a point a if and only if for every sequence x_n→a we have f(x_n)→f(a).
short: Continuity is the preservation of all convergent sequences.
long: Continuity is the preservation of all convergent sequences. In general topological spaces one needs sequences replaced by nets, but metric spaces are sequential.
proof: If f is epsilon-delta continuous, eventually x_n is within delta of a; conversely failure of continuity lets one choose a sequence x_n within 1/n of a whose images stay away from f(a).
consequence: It makes continuity easy to test using explicit sequences and explains the sequential definition of closed sets.

title: The Heine–Cantor Theorem on Uniform Continuity
subject: Real Analysis
statement: Every continuous function on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous.
latex: f\in C(K),\ K \text{ compact} \Rightarrow f \text{ uniformly continuous}
short: On a compact domain, one epsilon-delta choice works everywhere at once.
long: On a compact domain, one epsilon-delta choice works everywhere at once. The function 1/x on (0,1) shows compactness cannot simply be dropped.
proof: For each point choose a local delta by continuity; finitely many balls of half that radius cover the compact space, and a Lebesgue number argument gives a global delta.
consequence: It guarantees Riemann integrability of continuous functions on compact intervals.

title: Darboux's Theorem on the Intermediate Value Property of Derivatives
subject: Real Analysis
statement: Every derivative has the intermediate value property even when it is not continuous.
latex: f' \text{ satisfies the intermediate value property}
short: Derivatives cannot jump over values even if they are discontinuous.
long: Derivatives cannot jump over values even if they are discontinuous. This is why discontinuous derivatives, like x² sin(1/x²) at zero, must still take every intermediate value.
proof: For a value between f'(a) and f'(b), the function f(x)−cx has a local extremum in (a,b) for a suitable slope c; Fermat's theorem then gives a point where f'=c.
consequence: It shows derivatives form a restricted class of functions and motivates the study of Baire class one functions.

title: The Inverse Function Theorem in One Variable
subject: Real Analysis
statement: If f is continuously differentiable near a and f'(a) is nonzero, then f is locally invertible with differentiable inverse satisfying (f^{-1})'(f(a))=1/f'(a).
short: A nonzero derivative guarantees a local differentiable inverse.
long: A nonzero derivative guarantees a local differentiable inverse. Global invertibility needs additional hypotheses, such as strict monotonicity.
proof: The derivative's sign is constant near a, so f is strictly monotone there; applying the definition of derivative to the difference quotient of the inverse gives the reciprocal formula.
consequence: It is the one-dimensional model for the multivariable inverse function theorem and implicit function theorem.

title: L'Hôpital's Rule for Indeterminate Limits
subject: Real Analysis
statement: If f and g tend to zero or both to infinity and g' is nonzero near a, then the limit of f/g equals the limit of f'/g' whenever the latter exists.
short: For 0/0 and infinity/infinity limits, differentiate numerator and denominator.
long: For 0/0 and infinity/infinity limits, differentiate numerator and denominator. The existence of the derivative-ratio limit is required; the rule can fail without it.
proof: In the 0/0 case, Cauchy's mean value theorem gives f(x)/g(x)=f'(c)/g'(c) for some c between x and a, and then let x approach a.
consequence: It is a convenient computational tool but must be applied only to genuine indeterminate forms.

title: Upper and Lower Riemann Sums
subject: Real Analysis
statement: For a bounded function on a closed interval, the upper and lower sums over a partition use suprema and infima on subintervals; the function is Riemann integrable when their infimum and supremum over partitions agree.
short: Integrability means the best upper and lower approximations meet.
long: Integrability means the best upper and lower approximations meet. Continuous functions and monotone functions on closed intervals are Riemann integrable.
proof: Refining a partition decreases upper sums and increases lower sums; equality of the limiting values defines the integral, and the criterion follows by bounding the difference of any two sums.
consequence: It gives a precise criterion for integrability and explains why discontinuous functions may still be integrable.

title: Absolute versus Conditional Convergence of Improper Integrals
subject: Real Analysis
statement: An improper integral converges absolutely if the integral of the absolute value is finite, and conditionally if the integral converges but not absolutely.
short: Absolute convergence is robust; conditional convergence depends on cancellation.
long: Absolute convergence is robust; conditional convergence depends on cancellation. The integral of sin(x)/x from 1 to infinity converges conditionally.
proof: The inequality |∫f| ≤ ∫|f| and the Cauchy criterion for improper integrals give absolute convergence implies convergence.
consequence: It determines when rearrangement and domination arguments are legitimate.

title: Lebesgue Measure and Measurable Functions
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A Lebesgue measurable function is one for which the preimage of every Borel set is a measurable set, allowing integration with respect to Lebesgue measure.
latex: f^{-1}(B) \text{ measurable for all Borel } B
short: Measurability is the condition needed for the Lebesgue integral to make sense.
long: Measurability is the condition needed for the Lebesgue integral to make sense. Lebesgue measure extends length and is countably additive on the sigma-algebra of measurable sets.
proof: The class of measurable functions is closed under sums, products and limits because the corresponding operations on preimages stay within a sigma-algebra.
consequence: It supports the powerful convergence theorems unavailable for the Riemann integral.

title: The Monotone Convergence Theorem for Integrals
subject: Real Analysis
statement: For a pointwise increasing sequence of nonnegative measurable functions converging to f, the integrals converge to the integral of f, possibly infinite.
short: For nonnegative increasing functions, limits and integrals commute.
long: For nonnegative increasing functions, limits and integrals commute. The nonnegativity hypothesis is essential and is removed in the dominated convergence theorem by adding a dominating function.
proof: For the lower bound use that simple functions below f are eventually below f_n up to epsilon; the upper bound follows from monotonicity of the integral.
consequence: It is the key step in constructing the Lebesgue integral from simple functions.

title: Fatou's Lemma for Nonnegative Functions
subject: Real Analysis
statement: For a sequence of nonnegative measurable functions, the integral of the pointwise limit inferior is at most the limit inferior of the integrals.
short: Mass can disappear in a limit but cannot be created from nothing.
long: Mass can disappear in a limit but cannot be created from nothing. A moving spike of unit area converging pointwise to zero shows the inequality can be strict.
proof: Write liminf f_n as a pointwise increasing supremum of infima of tails and apply monotone convergence together with monotonicity of the integral.
consequence: It is used to prove dominated convergence and to establish lower semicontinuity of integral functionals.

title: Fubini's Theorem for Iterated Integrals
subject: Real Analysis
statement: If f is integrable on a product measure space, its iterated integrals exist and equal the integral over the product.
short: For absolutely integrable functions, the order of integration can be swapped.
long: For absolutely integrable functions, the order of integration can be swapped. The integrability hypothesis cannot simply be omitted for signed functions.
proof: Prove it first for characteristic functions of measurable rectangles, extend by linearity to simple functions, then by monotone convergence to nonnegative functions and finally by splitting into positive and negative parts.
consequence: It is the workhorse of probability, Fourier analysis and PDE.

title: Tonelli's Theorem for Nonnegative Functions
subject: Real Analysis
statement: For a nonnegative measurable function on a product of sigma-finite measure spaces, the iterated integrals exist and equal the product integral, possibly infinite.
short: Nonnegativity alone justifies swapping integration order.
long: Nonnegativity alone justifies swapping integration order. Tonelli's theorem is often used to check the integrability hypothesis needed for Fubini's theorem.
proof: Approximate f by increasing simple functions, apply the result to rectangles and pass to the limit via monotone convergence.
consequence: It allows computation of double integrals without first proving finiteness.

title: The Radon–Nikodym Theorem
subject: Real Analysis
statement: If a sigma-finite measure nu is absolutely continuous with respect to a sigma-finite measure mu, there is a measurable density f with nu(A)=integral over A of f dmu, unique up to mu-almost everywhere equality.
short: Absolute continuity means one measure is obtained from another by multiplying by a density.
long: Absolute continuity means one measure is obtained from another by multiplying by a density. The density f is called the Radon–Nikodym derivative and written dν/dμ.
proof: Use the Hahn decomposition and a maximality argument on functions whose integrals are bounded by nu, or apply the Hilbert space proof in the finite case via the Riesz representation theorem.
consequence: It generalises density functions and is essential in probability, ergodic theory and conditional expectation.

title: The Hahn–Banach Theorem
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A linear functional defined on a subspace of a normed vector space and dominated by a sublinear function extends to the whole space with the domination preserved.
latex: p(x)\ge f(x) \text{ on } M \Rightarrow \exists F:\ F|_M=f,\ F\le p
short: Bounded linear functionals can always be extended off a subspace.
long: Bounded linear functionals can always be extended off a subspace. A norm-preserving extension to the whole space follows by taking p(x)=||f|| ||x||.
proof: Zorn's lemma gives a maximal dominated extension; if its domain is not the whole space, one can extend by one more dimension while preserving dominance, contradicting maximality.
consequence: It guarantees enough continuous linear functionals to separate points and underlies duality theory.

title: The Uniform Boundedness Principle
subject: Real Analysis
statement: For a family of bounded linear operators between Banach spaces, pointwise boundedness implies uniform boundedness of their operator norms.
short: If operators are bounded at each point, their norms are bounded overall.
long: If operators are bounded at each point, their norms are bounded overall. Completeness of the domain is essential.
proof: The sets where the norms of the operators are at most n are closed and cover the space; Baire category gives one with nonempty interior, and scaling yields a uniform norm bound.
consequence: It proves pointwise convergence of bounded operators need not have bounded limits unless norms are uniformly bounded.

title: The Open Mapping Theorem for Banach Spaces
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A surjective bounded linear operator between Banach spaces is an open map.
short: Surjective continuous linear maps between complete spaces cannot shrink open sets to nowhere dense sets.
long: Surjective continuous linear maps between complete spaces cannot shrink open sets to nowhere dense sets. It implies that a bijective bounded linear operator between Banach spaces has bounded inverse.
proof: Write the domain as a countable union of scaled closed balls; Baire category gives one whose image has interior, and linearity plus iteration shows the image of the unit ball is a neighbourhood of zero.
consequence: It yields the bounded inverse theorem and equivalence of norms on finite-dimensional spaces.

title: The Closed Graph Theorem
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A linear operator between Banach spaces whose graph is closed in the product topology is bounded.
short: Closedness of the graph is enough to force continuity in the Banach setting.
long: Closedness of the graph is enough to force continuity in the Banach setting. The graph is closed exactly when x_n→x and Tx_n→y imply Tx=y.
proof: The projection from the graph to the domain is a continuous bijection between Banach spaces; the open mapping theorem makes its inverse bounded, giving a bound on T.
consequence: It is a convenient criterion for continuity of operators defined by closed differential expressions.

title: The Baire Category Theorem
subject: Real Analysis
statement: In a complete metric space, the intersection of countably many dense open sets is dense.
latex: \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty U_n \text{ dense for open dense } U_n
short: A complete space cannot be a countable union of nowhere dense pieces.
long: A complete space cannot be a countable union of nowhere dense pieces. Equivalently a nonempty complete metric space is not meagre in itself.
proof: Given any ball, choose nested closed balls of shrinking radii avoiding the complements of the dense open sets; completeness gives a point in their intersection inside the original ball.
consequence: It underlies the open mapping, closed graph and uniform boundedness theorems.

title: The Riesz Representation Theorem for Hilbert Spaces
subject: Real Analysis
statement: Every continuous linear functional on a Hilbert space has the form f(x)=inner product of x with a fixed vector y, with ||f||=||y||.
short: Hilbert space duals are identifiable with the space itself.
long: Hilbert space duals are identifiable with the space itself. The identification is conjugate-linear in the complex case.
proof: If f is nonzero, choose z orthogonal to ker f; every x decomposes as x=u+λz with u in ker f, and f(x)=λf(z) equals the inner product with a suitable multiple of z.
consequence: It is the abstract basis for weak formulations of PDEs and for the bra-ket notation of quantum mechanics.

title: Parseval's Identity in Hilbert Spaces
subject: Real Analysis
statement: For an orthonormal basis {e_n} of a Hilbert space, the sum of squared magnitudes of the Fourier coefficients equals the squared norm of the vector.
short: A vector's length equals the length of its coordinate list.
long: A vector's length equals the length of its coordinate list. The polarised version gives the inner product as a sum of products of coefficients.
proof: Approximate x by finite linear combinations of basis vectors; orthonormality makes the squared norm of the partial sum the partial sum of squared coefficients, and completeness passes to the limit.
consequence: It explains energy conservation for Fourier series and the unitarity of the Fourier transform.

title: The Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality
subject: Real Analysis
statement: For vectors in an inner product space, the absolute value of the inner product is at most the product of the norms, with equality exactly for linearly dependent vectors.
short: Correlations never exceed the product of individual sizes.
long: Correlations never exceed the product of individual sizes. It implies the triangle inequality for norms induced by inner products.
proof: For real t the quadratic ||x+ty||² is nonnegative; requiring its discriminant to be nonpositive gives the inequality, and equality corresponds to a double root.
consequence: It is ubiquitous in analysis, probability and statistics.

title: Minkowski's Inequality for Lp Norms
subject: Real Analysis
statement: For p at least one, the Lp norm satisfies ||f+g||_p ≤ ||f||_p + ||g||_p.
short: The Lp norm obeys the triangle inequality.
long: The Lp norm obeys the triangle inequality. Together with homogeneity it makes Lp a normed space, complete when p is at least one.
proof: Split |f+g|^p using |f+g| ≤ |f|+|g|, apply Hölder's inequality to the two resulting terms and divide by the appropriate power of ||f+g||_p.
consequence: It establishes the triangle inequality for Lp spaces, essential for functional analysis.

title: Hölder's Inequality for Conjugate Exponents
subject: Real Analysis
statement: If p and q satisfy 1/p+1/q=1, then the integral of |fg| is at most the product of the Lp and Lq norms.
short: Conjugate exponents give the sharp bound on the product of two functions.
long: Conjugate exponents give the sharp bound on the product of two functions. Equality holds when |f|^p and |g|^q are proportional almost everywhere.
proof: Apply Young's inequality ab ≤ a^p/p + b^q/q to normalised versions of |f| and |g| and integrate.
consequence: It implies Cauchy–Schwarz for p=q=2 and underpins duality of Lp spaces.

title: Jensen's Inequality for Convex Functions
subject: Real Analysis
statement: For a convex function φ and a random variable X, φ of the expectation is at most the expectation of φ(X).
short: Convexity says averaging inputs lowers the function value.
long: Convexity says averaging inputs lowers the function value. For concave functions the inequality reverses.
proof: A convex function lies below every supporting line; choose a supporting line at the mean and take expectations of both sides.
consequence: It proves AM–GM, power mean inequalities and risk aversion in economics.

title: The Weierstrass M-Test for Uniform Convergence
subject: Real Analysis
statement: If the terms of a series of functions are bounded by positive constants M_n with sum M_n finite, then the series converges uniformly.
short: A convergent numerical majorant controls an entire function series at once.
long: A convergent numerical majorant controls an entire function series at once. It gives uniform convergence but is only a sufficient condition.
proof: For any epsilon the tail of sum M_n is small, so the tail of sum f_n is uniformly small by the triangle inequality; the Cauchy criterion for uniform convergence applies.
consequence: It justifies termwise integration and differentiation of many power series and Fourier series.
